Present Perfect vs.The Simple Past Tense

You use the Present Perfect for actions which started in the past and are still happening now OR for finished actions which have a connection to the present.

You use the Simple Past for past events or actions which have no connection to the present.

Present Perfect Continuous vs. Present Perfect

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now. To emphasize the result of the action, use the simple form.
  • Has anyone called the police?

You use Present Perfect Continuous tense to describe:
  • a single activity that lasts a long time, and
  • an action that is repeated over a long period of time.
    • These continue up to the present. You can use the Present Perfect Continuous tense when a long activity has just stopped.
    To emphasize the action, use the continuous form.
    • What have the other people in the cafe been doing?

images.text:
Would you like to go to bed while a soothing voice whispered a lesson into your sleeping ears?

It has come to light that people all over the world have been trying out the new "learn while you sleep" method to study all sorts of subjects. English appears to be one of them. Specialists have run a number of experiments.

The fact the participants in the study have been learning three times more than they can during the day can't be ignored. Learning in their sleep has helped them to achieve far more than expected!

Language learners using this method have been able to do in at an amazing speed. These students haven't been spending time staring into space in the evening when they should be studying, they have been out enjoying themselves! Unfortunately, sleep learning tends to help you only remember things that you've already learned while awake.

In the study, specialists experimented by teaching people English over the radio. Students did ten lessons every two weeks. Before they went to sleep, they completed one lesson in English grammar and vocabulary. Then, peaceful music put them to sleep. A quiet voice whispered the lesson over again while they were slumbering.

Learning while you sleep may sound illogical, but, it seems to work. So if learning English is at the top of your list, there may come a day when you may find yourself learning it while in deep repose.
